1.text:
Is Our Universe the Only One?

Welcome to Deck 22 of the speculative science unit. Today's topics are strings, multiverses and simulations. The ideas get wilder, and the evidence gets thinner.

Keep your Evidence Meter out. Every claim gets a label: Established Fact, Plausible Hypothesis, Informed Speculation or Unknown. Today's big question: is our universe the only one?

2.text:
Is Our Universe the Only One?

Which statement do you agree with most? Pick one box.

There is one universe, and this is it. There are many universes we can never visit. We can never know, so it is not a science question. We might be living inside a computer simulation.

Be ready to defend your pick with evidence, not just a feeling. You'll come back to it at the end of the deck.

3.text:
Today I Can...

This is your checklist. Copy these as "I can" statements and rate yourself at the end.

I can explain why gravity and quantum physics don't fit together. I can describe string theory's main idea in plain words. I can explain why extra dimensions could stay hidden. I can use LHC results to judge string theory's predictions. I can compare string theory with loop quantum gravity. I can give the evidence for inflation.

I can explain eternal inflation and bubble universes. I can describe the many-worlds idea and why it's hard to test. I can explain fine-tuning and the anthropic principle. I can describe how a multiverse could be tested. I can summarize the simulation argument and its tests. And I can label each idea on the Evidence Meter. These connect to Indiana standards ES.1.2 and ES.1.3 and NGSS Practice 7, plus some enrichment.

4.text:
Two Great Theories That Don't Fit

Physics has two champion theories. General relativity explains gravity: planets, black holes, the expanding universe. It has passed every test so far: GPS, LIGO, the EHT images. ESTABLISHED FACT.

Quantum mechanics explains the very small: atoms, light, lasers, computer chips. It has passed every test so far, to extreme precision. ESTABLISHED FACT.

The trouble starts at the extremes. Inside a black hole, or at the very start of the Big Bang, you need both at once, and the math breaks. One theory that joins them, called quantum gravity, does not exist yet. UNKNOWN.

5.text:
Part 1: String Theory

What if everything is made of tiny vibrating strings? That's the idea behind one of the most famous attempts at quantum gravity.

Keep this question in mind: can an idea be beautiful math and still not be tested science?

6.text:
The Idea: Vibrating Strings

String theory says every particle is really a tiny vibrating loop or strand. Different vibrations would show up as different particles, like notes on one guitar string. INFORMED SPECULATION.

Its math includes a particle for gravity, the graviton, automatically. That's a fact about the math, so it's an ESTABLISHED FACT. But strings would be far too small for any experiment we can build to see. INFORMED SPECULATION.

Whether nature really works this way: UNKNOWN. A model that fits the math isn't the same as one that has passed a test.

7.text:
Extra Dimensions

String theory needs 10 or 11 dimensions in all: 10 for string theory itself, and 11 for its cousin, M-theory. But we experience 3 dimensions of space plus time. ESTABLISHED FACT.

So where are the others? The extra dimensions would be curled up too small to notice. INFORMED SPECULATION. Picture a garden hose seen from far away: it looks like a line. Up close, an ant could walk around it.

People have looked. Lab tests of gravity found no extra dimensions down to 52 micrometers, thinner than a hair. ESTABLISHED FACT.

8.text:
Predictions on Trial

What has the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) told us? First, supersymmetry. Many string models predict "partner" particles. The LHC has found none so far. That null result is an ESTABLISHED FACT.

Second, the Higgs boson. It was found at the LHC in 2012, as the Standard Model predicted. But it's not a string-theory test. ESTABLISHED FACT.

Third, testing strings directly would need energies about a million billion times higher than the LHC. ESTABLISHED FACT. No null result has killed string theory, but some versions have been ruled out.

9.text:
A Rival: Loop Quantum Gravity

There are two attempts at quantum gravity, and neither has passed a test yet.

String theory says particles are tiny strings. It needs extra dimensions, 10 or 11 in total, and tries to explain all forces and particles. Loop quantum gravity says space itself is made of tiny loops. It needs no extra dimensions and tries to explain mostly gravity and space.

Is either one confirmed by experiment? No and no. Both get INFORMED SPECULATION. Having two rival ideas is normal in science before the data decide.

10.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 1

Remember what "theory" means in science. Is string theory a "theory" in the scientific sense, like the theory of gravity?

Is it A) yes, because it has passed many tests, B) not yet, because there's no confirmed test so far, C) no, because math can never be science, or D) yes, because famous scientists support it? Choose, and explain what's wrong with the others.

11.text:
Part 2: The Multiverse

Could our universe be one bubble among many? We'll start with inflation, which has real evidence, then move to ideas with less and less.

Keep this question in mind: can we test something we can never visit?

12.text:
Inflation: The Best-Supported Step

Inflation is a super-fast stretching of space in the first tiny fraction of a second. You met it in Deck 19.

The CMB is the same temperature in every direction, to about 1 part in 100,000. ESTABLISHED FACT. Space is measured to be very nearly flat. ESTABLISHED FACT. Inflation explains both, and its predicted ripple pattern matches Planck data. It's strongly supported, a PLAUSIBLE HYPOTHESIS.

In 2014, BICEP2 claimed inflation's gravity-wave signal. It turned out to be dust. ESTABLISHED FACT. That's science correcting itself.

Did you know? Alan Guth proposed inflation in 1980 to explain why the universe is so smooth and flat.

13.text:
Eternal Inflation and Bubble Universes

Eternal inflation: in some models, inflation never fully stops. It keeps going in most of space. INFORMED SPECULATION.

Bubble universes: each region where inflation stops becomes its own "bubble," maybe with different physics. Picture a foam of soap bubbles, with our universe as just one. INFORMED SPECULATION.

Can we see them? Other bubbles would sit beyond anything we could ever observe. UNKNOWN.

14.text:
Many Worlds?

In 1957, Hugh Everett proposed the many-worlds interpretation. It's a different kind of "multiverse," about what quantum math means.

Quantum math predicts the odds of each outcome. Those odds are tested to high precision. ESTABLISHED FACT. Many-worlds says every outcome really happens, each in its own branch of reality. Flip a quantum coin, and both results happen in different branches. INFORMED SPECULATION.

But no experiment so far can tell many-worlds apart from other interpretations. ESTABLISHED FACT.

15.text:
Fine-Tuning and the Anthropic Principle

Change some forces a little, and stars or atoms might not form. This is fine-tuning. How fine the tuning really is gets debated, so it's a PLAUSIBLE HYPOTHESIS.

The weak anthropic principle says we can only observe a universe that allows observers. So it's no surprise ours allows life. It's a logic point, not an experiment. As philosophy, it's INFORMED SPECULATION.

The multiverse answer: there are many universes, each with different settings. We live in one of the rare ones that allow life. The other universes can't be observed. INFORMED SPECULATION.

16.text:
How Scientists Test a Multiverse

Oddly enough, some multiverse ideas do make a testable prediction. The test goes like this. 1, Predict: if our bubble once bumped another, it could leave a round spot in the CMB. 2, Look: search the WMAP and Planck maps for round patterns. 3, Compare: are any spots stronger than random noise? 4, Result: no bubble collision found so far. 5, Next: better maps, and the hunt for inflation's B-modes.

A 2011 search of WMAP data found no convincing bubble collision. ESTABLISHED FACT. A null result does not rule the multiverse out. ESTABLISHED FACT. Finding a collision would be strong evidence for other bubbles. PLAUSIBLE HYPOTHESIS.

Your turn: is an idea that can never be tested still science?

17.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 2

Separate real evidence from wild guesses. Which observation is real evidence for inflation?

Is it A) the CMB is nearly the same temperature everywhere, B) we have photographed other universes, C) string theory proved it, or D) the LHC made a bubble universe? Use Slide 12 to decide.

18.text:
Part 3: The Simulation Hypothesis

Could we be living inside a computer? This idea started in philosophy, not physics. Watch how scientists try to make it testable.

Keep this question in mind: what evidence could ever settle this?

19.text:
Bostrom's Argument

The simulation argument is a 2003 philosophy argument by Nick Bostrom. Bostrom argued one of 3 is likely true: civilizations rarely reach the tech to simulate whole worlds, they choose not to run such simulations, or we are probably in one.

That he argued it is an ESTABLISHED FACT. Notice that he doesn't say we ARE in a simulation, just that one of the three is likely. The argument rests on guesses about future computers and future people. INFORMED SPECULATION.

Whether we actually live in a simulation: UNKNOWN.

20.text:
A Proposed Test

In 2012, Beane, Davoudi and Savage proposed a cosmic-ray test. If space were a grid of points, the highest-energy cosmic rays might favor certain directions. INFORMED SPECULATION.

No experiment has found any sign that we live in a simulation. ESTABLISHED FACT. But a perfect simulation might hide every clue. UNKNOWN.

21.text:
Is It Falsifiable?

Scientists and philosophers really do debate this. The debate itself is an ESTABLISHED FACT.

Yes, maybe: some versions predict glitches or grid patterns. Those could be searched for, so those versions are testable. INFORMED SPECULATION. No: a perfect simulation could fake any result. Then no test could prove it wrong. That would put it outside science. INFORMED SPECULATION.

Think back to Deck 21 Slide 5: if nothing could ever prove an idea wrong, it fails the falsifiability check.

22.text:
Student Task: Four Corners Debate

Time to move! Each corner of the room is one Evidence Meter label: EF, PH, IS or UK. Mr. Dimitry reads a claim: strings, inflation, bubbles, many-worlds, simulation.

Walk to the label you pick and defend it with one piece of evidence. Switch corners if someone convinces you, and write down why.

Record two things: A, my corner: EF, PH, IS or UK. B, my best piece of evidence.

23.text:
Exit Ticket

Show what you learned about the edges of physics.

First, why do physicists want a theory of quantum gravity? Second, what has the LHC found, or not found, that matters for string theory? Third, give one piece of evidence for inflation. Fourth, how could scientists test for a bubble collision? Fifth, label it and explain: "We live in a simulation."

Then look back at your "I can" list from Slide 3 and rate yourself 1 to 3 on each one.

24.text:
The Standards Behind This Lesson

This lesson follows the Indiana Earth and Space Science standards, plus one science practice. Here's what they ask, in plain words.

ES.1.2: describe the expanding universe, or Big Bang Theory, using evidence: the Doppler effect, redshift, Hubble's Law and the cosmic microwave background. ES.1.3: make a diagram, flowchart or explanation of how energy cooled into protons and early elements, and how those elements formed huge stars and galaxies, with gravity pulling clouds together.

NGSS Science Practice 7: engaging in argument from evidence. Use evidence to defend or reject a claim, and judge how strong the evidence is.
